doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Hampton's practice habits, Giant Steps with Bags and touring
summary: Hampton practiced hours daily, called Giant Steps to challenge Milt Jackson in Detroit, and rehearsed after 15-hour bus rides; Davenport's advice proved right.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Yeah. And he would practice. Because where I stayed, it was at 63rd and Broadway. And he stayed on 64th and Broadway at Lincoln Plaza. And I used to go up to his house every day. And he would go through some stuff. He was an old man then, he was about 76 or something, 75 or 76. And he was still practicing 4 to 5 hours a day. And one time we went to Detroit at the Pontchartrain Hotel. And then Gates called “Giant Steps.” And Bags had come up there with his vibes. First they did this “I’ve Got Rhythm” thing, I think it was Hamp and Dex we used to call it, Eric Dickerson — not Eric Dickerson, who was the tenor player?
Eric Dixon, yeah. I’m thinking Eric Dickerson the football player. Eric Dixon had done an arrangement that Dexter Gordon and Hampton had done on that, and boy —

It was “I’ve Got Rhythm,” Gates stepped in. And they did that first. And Bags played really well. But boy then Lionel Hampton really wanted blood. He said, “Kid get out that ‘Giant Steps’” boys.” Boy, Gates started playing that minor third and perfect fourth man

and oh my goodness. And Bags was like, you know Bags is a great bluesy player, but he didn’t play those kinds of changes. Man, Gates just wanted blood man. But it was so exciting though. You know we’d have a ride from New Haven to, I don’t know, Chicago or somewhere like that. As soon as you get out of the bus — Gates would fly — hey man, you’re on the bus 15 hours. And he’d say, “It’s time for a rehearsal.” So I mean you’d get out there dog tired, red eyed, and 15 guys on the bus with one urinal, you know.
